note: Per docs/roadmap.md's resume contract: never edit a committed observation to look better. This file corrects an analytical error in measurement-summary.json's root_causes_observed field, found on review; the measured numbers themselves (Must/May/Unknown counts, precision, recall) are unaffected and unchanged.

corrections.original_claim: "Must proofs are restricted to same-file, top-level, direct-binding calls ... the trustworthiness fixtures' tests live in the same file as the mutated function but every test function's own assert_eq!/similar macro invocation is an 'unexpanded-macro-or-decorator' Unknown claim ..."
corrections.problem: Factually wrong: the fixtures' tests do NOT live in the same file as the mutated function. Verified via `find fixtures/core-trustworthiness -type f`: Rust mutates fixtures/core-trustworthiness/rust/baseline/src/operations.rs but its tests live in fixtures/core-trustworthiness/rust/baseline/tests/impact.rs (a separate integration-test file, per Rust's own convention). Python mutates .../python/baseline/models.py but its tests live in .../python/baseline/tests/test_service.py, as methods of a class (OracleTests) — confirmed by the graph_paths pattern crate::tests::test_service::OracleTests::{test} used in tools/core_trustworthiness_oracle.py.
corrections.corrected_explanation: Two independent, already-documented root causes apply, not the same-file macro claim: (1) the cross-file limitation already correctly stated elsewhere in measurement-summary.json's root_causes_observed list — annotate() runs once per file during extraction, before project-wide resolve_calls, so a call's target must be declared in the SAME file to be provable Must; both fixtures' tests call their mutated function from a different file, so neither could reach Must regardless of any macro invocation. (2) For Python specifically, the extractor's proof rule is also restricted to *top-level* function declarations (crates/aether-builder/src/mapper/claims.rs's `top` collection only walks direct children of the module root); OracleTests's test methods are class methods, not top-level, so they are excluded by that rule independently of the cross-file issue — even a same-file class-method test could not reach Must under the current extractor.
corrections.does_assert_eq_still_matter: Yes, but not as the primary cause claimed originally: assert_eq!/similar macro invocations inside a test function do still produce their own 'unexpanded-macro-or-decorator' Unknown claim on that test's own outgoing calls, and (per aether-graph/src/claims.rs's whole-graph flood rule) any Unknown claim anywhere is sufficient to flood every function in the graph to at least Unknown. So the macro-invocation observation is real and does independently guarantee the flood fires — it was just not the reason the *specific* must-proof from test to mutated-function failed, which was cross-file/non-top-level from the start.

corrections.original_claim: "cross-file calls (the Click Group.invoke mutation, and Go's TestAdd/Add split across files) can never reach Must"
corrections.problem: The Go TestAdd/Add example was a manual reproduction against a hand-written two-file fixture used to check the extractor's behavior during implementation (see the cli.rs integration test test_impact_quiet_includes_go_test_names_and_builds_its_run_command); it was not part of either measured corpus (core-trustworthiness has no Go fixture, and core-representative-mutations measures only Click/Python). Citing it alongside Click's measured result implied it was measured evidence.
corrections.corrected_explanation: The cross-file claim itself is correct and applies to Click's measured Group.invoke mutation (verified: crate::click::core::Group::invoke's declared callers in tests/test_commands.py and tests/test_chain.py are in different files from src/click/core.py). The Go case is a plausible-but-unmeasured illustration of the same general limitation, not corpus evidence; Stage 2's dispatch corpus is expected to add a measured Go case.
